articles.author: Antonios Thanasis
articles.description:
Upgrading a production database? Don't make production your test environment.
A safer approach is to restore production to a separate Azure MySQL server, test the upgrade there, and only then upgrade production.
Production MySQL 5.7
        ↓
Restore to separate test server
        ↓
Verify server
        ↓
Run MySQL Upgrade Checker
        ↓
Fix compatibility issues
        ↓
Upgrade test server to MySQL 8.0
        ↓
Test application
        ↓
Upgrade production

Create a separate Azure MySQL server from a recent production backup or point-in-time restore.
Your production database remains untouched while you test the upgrade.
Connect to the test server, not production, using MySQL Shell:
\connect user@server.mysql.database.azure.com
\js

Verify where you're connected:
SELECT @@hostname, @@version;

Then run the Upgrade Checker:
util.checkForServerUpgrade({
  targetVersion: "8.0"
})

The checker identifies known compatibility issues that should be addressed before upgrading.
Important: The Upgrade Checker is not a replacement for application testing.
Once the reported issues are addressed, upgrade the test server to MySQL 8.0.
Then point your application to the test database and test:
Queries
Migrations
APIs
Queues and jobs
Authentication
Stored procedures/events, if used
Application functionality
Performance
If the test upgrade succeeds and your application behaves correctly, prepare your production backup and maintenance plan, then perform the production upgrade.
Restore → Check → Fix → Upgrade → Test → Upgrade production
The key rule is simple:
Never make production your first upgrade test. 🚀
articles.title: Safely Test a MySQL 5.7 -> 8.0 Upgrade on Azure

Containers limit blast radius. They do not prevent an autonomous coding agent from reading a secret in one tool call and exfiltrating it via an outbound network call in the next, all within the same approved session. They do not stop force pushes to protected branches. They do not prevent irreversible commands during unattended runs.
The question is not whether to gate shell access. The question is how to build a gate that does not break legitimate agent workflows while blocking destructive operations, and what happens when the gate itself fails.
Running an agent in a container provides process isolation and filesystem boundaries. It does not provide semantic command control.
What containers give you:
Process namespace isolation
Filesystem mount restrictions
Network policy enforcement at t…
articles.title: Gating Agent Shell Access: Why Containers Aren't Enough and Approval Loops Break

articles.author: mech.app
articles.description:
Local development usually means localhost:3000, localhost:8080, and a mental map of which port belongs to which service. AI agents struggle with this. They cannot reliably track dynamic port assignments across restarts, and they cannot predict which port a framework will choose when you spin up a new service.
Portless replaces port numbers with stable .localhost URLs. Instead of http://localhost:3000, you get https://myapp.localhost. The tool handles TLS, port assignment, and framework-specific CLI flag injection so your services bind to the right port without manual configuration.
It hit 12,000 GitHub stars in days and ranked #3 on TypeScript trending. The reason is simple: it solves a coordination problem that gets worse as you add more services or more agents to your workflow.
